Probably not at 100%, and the "single fund = diversified" premise is the weak part. It's 500 stocks, but one asset class, one country, and heavily concentrated: the top 10 holdings have been roughly a third or more of the index.

The main risk at 56 is sequence-of-returns risk. A deep drawdown in the years just before or after retirement does disproportionate damage because you're about to start withdrawing or stop contributing. The S&P 500 fell about 50% in 2000-02 and about 55% in 2007-09, and the 2000-2012 stretch was roughly flat in real terms. If that happens at 62-65, you can't wait it out as easily as a 30-year-old can.

The case for it is real: a 30+ year horizon, low fees, and historically strong long-run returns. If Social Security, a pension, or other guaranteed income covers your essential expenses, you can carry more equity risk than the usual rules suggest. The question isn't "is stock exposure good" but "can I hold through a 50% drop without selling, and does my plan survive it?"

Concretely:
- A mix with bonds or cash for the next several years of withdrawals, plus a total-market or international fund, is the standard hedge. Many people your age hold roughly 60-80% equities, but that depends on your situation.
- Moving everything at once also locks in a market-timing bet. If this is a taxable account, selling triggers capital gains; in an IRA or 401(k) it doesn't.
- This would change if you plan to work to 67+, have large guaranteed income, or have a big savings surplus relative to your needs. It would get worse if you'd need to start drawing on this money within about 10 years and have little other income.

Without your retirement date, other income, and savings relative to spending, I can't say what the right allocation is. A fee-only fiduciary planner can stress-test it against your actual numbers.
